The White-backed vulture (Gyps africanus) exhibits a slow life history, typical of large Accipitrid scavengers. Females lay a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and, under favorable conditions, may produce only one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year], resulting in a maximum annual reproductive output of one offspring per breeding pair annually. This low fecundity reflects the extreme energetic demands of raising a single, large chick. The average egg weighs approximately 220 grams, and newly hatched nestlings typically display a wet weight at birth of 200 grams [Wwb = 200 grams]. These neonatal chicks are altricial but rapidly gain mass, requiring consistent parental brooding at an optimal temperature near 36 °C [T = 36 °C] for proper thermoregulation and development; under these conditions, the age at birth corresponds to an incubation period of 55 days [ab = 55 days]. This extended incubation duration is among the longest recorded for any accipitrid vulture of comparable body size.

As the nestling progresses, its growth trajectory is steep, fueled by extensive biparental provisioning of carrion. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult White-backed vulture averages approximately 6200 grams [Wwi = approximately 6200 grams], with documented adult body mass typically ranging from 4.2 to 7.2 kg. This considerable adult mass is an adaptation for long-distance soaring flight and competitive dominance at carcasses. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of the active metabolic period (40 °C [T = 40 °C]), the time since birth at fledging is recorded at 125 days [tx = 125 days]. The achievement of sustained flight marks a critical developmental milestone, after which the fledgling begins to accompany adults to feeding sites, though it remains partially dependent on parental provisioning for several additional weeks. This period of flight feather maturation and muscle development is energetically costly.

Sexual maturation in this species is a notably prolonged process. Under the same thermal regime of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the time since birth at puberty is reached at 375 days [tp = 375 days], a value that represents the onset of reproductive capability and gonadal activity. Despite reaching this physiological threshold, young vultures do not typically engage in breeding immediately. Instead, they may undergo a period of social learning and territory prospecting, delaying their first successful breeding attempt. The time since birth at first brood, marking the age at which an individual produces its first clutch, is considerably later, estimated at 1460 days [tR = 1460 days] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This four-year delay between physiological puberty and actual first reproduction is a common life-history strategy among long-lived bird species, allowing individuals to acquire the foraging competence and social status necessary for successful nesting.

Longevity data for the White-backed vulture indicate a substantial lifespan, with the oldest documented individuals reaching approximately 19.7 years in natural conditions. At an ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the maximum documented lifespan corresponds to 19.7 years [am = 19.7 years], a duration that aligns with the slow pace of life characteristic of large-bodied avian scavengers. This impressive longevity is facilitated by a relatively low extrinsic mortality rate once individuals reach adulthood, owing to their position as obligate scavengers with few natural predators. The species' life history is thus characterized by high adult survival, delayed reproduction, and a very low reproductive rate, all of which render the population particularly vulnerable to anthropogenic threats such as poisoning and habitat degradation. Senescence in this species is poorly documented but is believed to involve gradual reproductive decline in the final years of life.

The ecological role of the White-backed vulture as an obligate scavenger is intimately linked to its life-history parameters. The single-egg clutch [N_R_i = single-egg clutch] and solitary nesting habit, where only one clutch is attempted annually [F_R_i = one clutch is attempted annually], constrain the species' capacity for rapid population recovery following declines. In comparison with smaller, more fecund raptors, the annual reproductive output is exceptionally low, a trade-off for the extended parental care and large body size required for efficient competition at carcasses. Field observations at active nests have confirmed the incubation duration of 55 days [ab = 55 days] under a reliable brooding temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. The steady mass gain from the 200-gram hatchling (200 grams) [Wwb = 200 grams] to the fledgling stage, and eventually to the adult weight of 6200 grams [Wwi = 6200 grams], underscores the nutritional dependency on predictable, abundant carrion resources, which are increasingly scarce across the species' African range.
